tldr: By embedding contraction control feedback inside each rollout and verifying safety at runtime with a barrier function, this paper proposes a sampling-based MPC that simultaneously guarantees theoretical tracking stability and probabilistic safety, even with a small number of samples.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of CS-MPC. Offline, contraction metrics and gains are synthesized and certified along the nominal trajectory. Online, rollouts run internal feedback to bundle samples closely around the reference trajectory, and finally, a quantile-tightened discrete-time CBF verifies and corrects the applied input for safety.
overview:
For robot control under model uncertainty and dynamically revealed obstacles—such as planetary rovers traversing rough terrain, drones dodging moving obstacles, or spacecraft landing on asteroids—sampling-based MPC (especially MPPI: Model Predictive Path Integral control) is a powerful tool. It does not require gradient computation and naturally handles non-smooth cost functions and complex constraints.

However, conventional MPPI has critical weaknesses. Because rollouts are generated in an open-loop fashion, predicted trajectories disperse rapidly on unstable systems, demanding enormous sample sizes. Safety constraints can only be handled as soft penalties, offering no formal safety guarantee for the executed control inputs. Furthermore, the tracking error caused by having only a finite number of samples lacks theoretical analysis.

To solve this, the authors propose "CS-MPC", a two-layer architecture combining contraction theory with discrete-time control barrier functions (DCBFs). By running an offline-certified feedback controller inside every rollout, trajectory dispersion is suppressed even over long prediction horizons. In addition, the online weighted control input is verified by a DCBF tightened using the quantile of the one-step prediction error. If unsafe, the system switches to a verified safe sample input or a backup policy.

In simulation experiments, CS-MPC matched the tracking accuracy of standard MPPI with 7 to 20 times fewer rollouts on a rover, and achieved 2 to 4 times lower tracking error on a quadrotor. Across 200 Monte Carlo missions including asteroid landing, it incurred zero safety constraint violations, validating the derived stochastic stability bound that explicitly links sample count to tracking error.
contributions: Incorporating contraction-certified feedback inside every rollout, theoretically proving that trajectory dispersion is uniformly bounded irrespective of horizon length.

Constructing an execution-layer safety verification mechanism using discrete-time control barrier functions (DCBF) tightened by the quantile of the one-step prediction error under persistent parameter uncertainty and disturbances.

Deriving a concentration inequality for the weighted control input under finite samples ($N_s$), and proving closed-loop stochastic stability that explicitly decouples the impacts of sampling error, disturbances, and avoidance maneuvers on tracking error.
Demonstrating substantial improvements in sample efficiency and zero collisions across 200 mission trials in three nonlinear simulations: a rover, a quadrotor, and an asteroid landing.

sections.heading: Why Isn't Standard MPPI Enough?
sections.summary: While sampling-based MPC handles non-smooth, non-convex costs flexibly, it suffers from three challenges: rollout dispersion, lack of safety guarantees, and absence of finite-sample theoretical analysis. This paper resolves all three at once with CS-MPC, combining contraction-based closed-loop rollouts and discrete-time barrier function runtime verification.
sections.details:
Tracking trajectories in extreme environments where prior modeling is difficult—such as wheel slip in planetary rovers, gravity and rotation uncertainties in asteroid landers, or unknown moving obstacles encountered by drones—serves as the motivation for this work.

Sampling-based MPC (especially MPPI), which computes control inputs using Monte Carlo rollouts, is very popular for these tasks. It does not require gradients of the cost function and can directly evaluate non-smooth costs and discrete penalties. However, standard MPPI faces three fundamental bottlenecks:

- Rapid rollout dispersion: Propagating dynamics open-loop causes samples to scatter widely on unstable systems or over long horizons, requiring an astronomical number of samples to find viable control inputs.
- Lack of safety guarantees for executed inputs: Obstacle constraints are merely incorporated as penalty terms in the rollout cost function, offering no guarantee that the control input actually sent to the robot respects safety boundaries.
- Lack of theoretical guarantees: In realistic settings where only a finite number of samples can be used, the effect of sampling error on closed-loop tracking performance has lacked theoretical analysis.

CS-MPC resolves these with two layers. In the first "stability and performance layer", contraction feedback synthesized and certified along a nominal reference trajectory is applied inside every rollout, tightly bundling sample trajectories around the reference. In the second "execution layer", the input computed via MPPI importance weighting is verified against a discrete-time control barrier function (DCBF), falling back to a safe sample or a backup policy when necessary.

sections.heading: Prior Innovations and Where CS-MPC Fits In
sections.summary: While prior methods like Tube-MPPI and covariance-steering MPPI aim to tame sampling variance, none embed nonlinear feedback with an explicit contraction rate inside the rollouts. Furthermore, inspecting safety strictly on the post-averaged sample input right before execution using barrier functions is also a novel framework.
sections.details:
### Evolution and Limits of Sampling-Based MPC
To curb rollout dispersion in MPPI, prior work has explored Tube-MPPI with auxiliary tracking controllers, covariance-steering MPPI to constrain terminal variance, and learned proposals. However, these methods either apply feedback outside the rollouts or rely on local linearizations; none embed nonlinear feedback inside the rollouts with a certified contraction rate over an explicit state domain.

### Applications of Contraction Theory
Contraction theory assesses global incremental stability by analyzing the variational dynamics between system trajectories. While applied in MPC through approaches like tube MPC, conventional designs solving online convex optimizations cannot directly handle discontinuous or non-smooth costs like indicator functions or $\ell_0$ norms. This work achieves both non-smooth cost optimization and theoretical stability by certifying contraction of the nominal system via offline Riccati computations while using importance sampling for online cost evaluations.

### Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and Probabilistic Safety
CBFs are powerful tools to guarantee forward invariance of safe sets. However, the admissible control set under a nonlinear CBF is often non-convex. Consequently, even if every individual sample satisfies the safety condition, their importance-weighted average can easily violate the safe set. This work cleanly circumvents this issue by enforcing quantile-tightened discrete-time CBF conditions directly on the post-average "actually executed input".

sections.heading: What Control Problem Are We Trying to Solve?
sections.summary: The target is a nonlinear stochastic discrete-time system subject to persistent parameter errors fixed throughout the mission, white process noise, and actuator deadbands or quantization. The objective is to accurately track a nominal reference trajectory without violating dynamic safety constraints revealed online.
sections.details:
We consider the following discrete-time nonlinear stochastic system:
$$x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k) + \Delta f(x_k, u_k; \vartheta) + d_{a,k}(x_k, u_k) + w_k$$
Here, $x_k$ is the state, $u_k$ is the bounded control input, and $f$ is the known nominal model.

An essential feature of this formulation is the careful distinction between types of uncertainty:
- Persistent parameter error $\Delta f(x_k, u_k; \vartheta)$: Unknown parameters $\vartheta$, such as mass, inertia, or terrain friction, are chosen once at mission start and remain fixed throughout. Hence, they are temporally correlated (biased).
- Actuator error $d_{a,k}$: Nonlinear implementation errors such as deadbands or quantization.
- Process noise $w_k$: Zero-mean independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) disturbances.

Collectively, these are termed the "one-step prediction error" $d_{x,k}(u) := x_{k+1} - f(x_k, u)$. Because it carries temporal correlation, it must be treated as a conditional statistic.

The safe set is defined as $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{safe}}(t) := \{x \mid h_c(x, t) \geq 0\}$. Here, the barrier function $h_c$ is represented as the minimum ($\min$) of static constraints $h_s$ and dynamically predicted constraints $h_d$, which can capture non-convex obstacles and avoidance regions. The goal is to design a causal policy using a finite sample count $N_s$ that minimizes tracking error relative to the nominal reference trajectory while maintaining safety over the entire mission under a prescribed risk budget $\delta_{\mathrm{mis}}$.

sections.heading: Three Pillars of Theory: Information Structure, Contraction, and Barrier Functions
sections.summary: We define the information structure before and after sampling, and present certification conditions for contraction metrics and gains derived from discrete-time Riccati equations around the reference trajectory. In addition, discrete-time CBF tightening using quantile sets for the one-step prediction error under uncertainty is introduced.
sections.details:
### III-A Information Structure and Timing
To ensure mathematical rigor, we strictly distinguish between pre-sampling information $\mathcal{F}_k$ and post-perturbation-sampling information $\mathcal{H}_k$ at step $k$. This decouples the probability space associated with randomized sampling from that of the unknown disturbances $w_k$.

### III-B & III-C Applying Discrete-Time Contraction Theory
By solving discrete-time LQR Riccati equations backward in time around the reference trajectory $(\bar{x}_k, \bar{u}_k)$, we obtain time-varying metric matrices $M_k$ and feedback gains $K_k$. Letting $J_k(x)$ denote the Jacobian of the nominal closed-loop dynamics, we verify whether
$$J_k(x)^\top M_{k+1} J_k(x) \preceq \beta M_k$$
holds across the certification domain $\mathcal{X}$ with contraction rate $\beta < 1$. While the Riccati equation itself guarantees this only along the nominal trajectory, Proposition 1 derives conditions to certify it across the entire domain by bounding the Hessian terms.

### III-D Stochastic DCBF and MPPI Foundations
The discrete-time control barrier function (DCBF) condition requires that the safety margin one step ahead satisfies $h(x_{k+1}, t_{k+1}) \geq (1 - \alpha) h(x_k, t_k)$. Under uncertainty, this condition is tightened (shrunk) using a conditional quantile set $\mathcal{E}_k(u; \delta_k)$ that contains the prediction error $d_{x,k}(u)$ with probability at least $1 - \delta_k$. Allocating the per-step risk budget such that $\sum \delta_k \leq \delta_{\mathrm{mis}}$ theoretically certifies mission-level safety.

sections.heading: Designing CS-MPC: Contraction Rollouts and Runtime Safety Filtering
sections.summary: Running contraction feedback inside each rollout uniformly bounds sample dispersion regardless of horizon length. Furthermore, after computing a weighted input that accommodates non-smooth costs, runtime verification via a quantile-tightened DCBF selects and executes a safe control input.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Contraction Sampling Law and Rollout Dispersion Control
The rollout generation in CS-MPC takes the following form:
$$u_{i \mid k}^{(b)} = \Pi_{\mathcal{U}} \left( \bar{u}_{k+i} + K_{k+i} (\bar{x}_{k+i} \ominus x_{i \mid k}^{(b)}) + \mu_{i \mid k} + \varepsilon_{i \mid k}^{(b)} \right)$$
Crucially, the feedback gain $K$ is embedded directly within the rollout. In addition, deterministic anchors (mean, pure feedback, and backup) are included in the sample batch.

In Proposition 3, the expected spread $\varsigma_{i \mid k}^{(b)}$ of samples relative to the pure feedback trajectory is proven to have a uniform upper bound independent of horizon length $H$. While open-loop rollouts disperse exponentially on unstable systems, in CS-MPC the spread is geometrically suppressed by the contraction rate $\sqrt{\beta} < 1$, preventing sample dispersion even over long prediction horizons.

### IV-B1 Barrier-Aware Exploration Covariance Design
When approaching obstacles such that the predicted barrier value drops below a threshold, the method temporarily expands the isotropic exploration variance (by a factor $\zeta \geq 1$) or scales it along the contraction metric $M$, boosting exploration efficiency for avoidance maneuvers.

### IV-C & IV-D Cost Design and Runtime DCBF Filter
In addition to metric norms on tracking error and DCBF penalties, the rollout cost function can directly accommodate non-smooth control costs, such as the $\ell_0$ norm.

Right before execution, the weighted average input $u_k^{\mathrm{exec}}$ is verified against the following DCBF condition:
$$\inf_{d \in \widetilde{\mathcal{E}}_k} h(f(x_k, u) + d, t_{k+1}) \geq (1 - \alpha) h(x_k, t_k)$$
If the weighted input fails this condition, the system instead applies the passing sample input closest to the weighted average, or falls back to a backup policy such as gradient ascent on the barrier function (guaranteeing probabilistic safety via Proposition 4).

sections.heading: What Happens with Finite Samples? Proof of Stochastic Stability
sections.summary: We bound the gap between the finite-sample weighted input and its infinite-sample population counterpart using Hoeffding's inequality ($O(N_f^{-1/2})$). Propagating this sampling error through the contraction dynamics yields a finite-sample stochastic stability bound (Theorem 1) on the closed-loop mean-squared tracking error.
sections.details:
### V-A Concentration Inequality for the Weighted Input
Let $N_f = N_s - 3$ be the number of free samples. Lemma 1 evaluates the error between the MPPI finite-sample input $\widehat{u}_k$ and the ideal population input $u_k^{\circ}$ obtained as sample size approaches infinity.

Under bounded costs and an input space diameter $d_{\mathcal{U}}$, the following holds with probability at least $1 - \eta_s$:
$$\|\widehat{u}_k^{(N_f)} - u_k^{\circ,(N_f)}\|_2 \leq O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(m/\eta_s)}{N_f}}\right)$$
In short, the sampling-induced input error decays at the standard Monte Carlo rate of $N_f^{-1/2}$. Furthermore, Corollary 2 shows this constant can be tightened by restricting sampling to the neighborhood of the feedback input.

### V-B Closed-Loop Stochastic Stability Bound (Theorem 1)
By incorporating this finite-sample error alongside persistent prediction errors (bias and covariance) into the contraction system dynamics, we obtain the primary result, Theorem 1. The executed mean-squared tracking error satisfies the following recursion:
$$\mathbb{E}[\|e_{k+1}\|_{M_{k+1}}^2] \leq \beta_{\mathrm{fs}} \mathbb{E}[\|e_k\|_{M_k}^2] + c_{\mathrm{alg}} + c_{d,k}^{\mathrm{exec}}$$
Here, the contraction rate $\beta_{\mathrm{fs}} < 1$ is governed by the nominal contraction rate, and the asymptotic error floor cleanly decouples into an algorithmic error $c_{\mathrm{alg}}$ that decreases inversely with sample count $N_f$, and an uncertainty term $c_{d,k}^{\mathrm{exec}}$ from persistent parameter errors and disturbance covariance. This theoretically proves that increasing samples directly cuts down algorithmic tracking error.

sections.heading: Validated on Three Demanding Robotic Simulations
sections.summary: We evaluated CS-MPC across three environments: a rover with terrain slip, a quadrotor under dynamic obstacles, and an asteroid landing (Bennu) with gravity and rotational uncertainty. CS-MPC achieved dramatic sample efficiency (7 to 20 times) and superior tracking accuracy over conventional MPPI, with zero collisions over 200 missions.
sections.details:
### VI-B Skid-Steer Rover (Wheel Slip Uncertainty)
A 7-state rover controlled via left/right wheel speed commands operates under surface friction parameters $\vartheta$ that vary per trial. The rover navigates between static obstacles and an oscillating non-convex obstacle.
- Results: CS-MPC achieved an RMS position tracking error of $0.52$ m with just $N_s = 15$ samples. Standard MPPI required $N_s = 100 \sim 300$ samples to reach equivalent accuracy, demonstrating roughly 7 to 20 times higher sample efficiency. Moreover, while MPPI experienced frequent collisions when $N_s \leq 10$, CS-MPC achieved zero collisions across all tested sample counts.

### VI-C Quadrotor (Figure-Eight Flight Under Dynamic Obstacles)
A 12-state unstable nonlinear quadrotor system tracks a figure-eight trajectory while dodging two moving spherical obstacles.
- Results: Across all sample counts from $N_s = 10$ to $1000$, CS-MPC achieved 2 to 4 times lower RMS position tracking error ($0.25 \sim 0.38$ m) than standard MPPI. Removing the execution layer reduced the tracking error slightly but dangerously eroded obstacle clearance, confirming that the runtime safety filter successfully maintains necessary safety margins.

### VI-D Asteroid Landing on Bennu
A spacecraft landing on asteroid Bennu under an unknown gravity field, rotational velocity, and mass concentrations (mascons), with thruster minimum-impulse-bit (deadband) constraints to minimize fuel use.
- Results: Under harsh conditions where a keep-out zone suddenly appears mid-descent, CS-MPC avoided the obstacle in 10 out of 10 trials (minimum clearance $6.3$ m) and achieved a landing error of $0.14$ m. In contrast, standard MPPI and pure feedback failed to avoid the obstacle and crashed.

### VI-E & VI-F Verification of Theoretical Bounds and Safety
In station-keeping experiments, the stability bound of Theorem 1 strictly upper-bounded the empirical mean energy (with a conservatism ratio of about 500 to 650), and the RMS input error decayed at the theoretical $N_f^{-1/2}$ rate. Across all 200 Monte Carlo missions, the empirical barrier violation rate was exactly 0%.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: CS-MPC brings contraction theory and barrier functions together for nonlinear systems under uncertainty. It simultaneously delivers finite-sample stochastic stability and mission-level safety, demonstrating overwhelming sample efficiency in realistic robotic tasks.
sections.details:
This work provides a solid theoretical foundation for sampling-based MPC (MPPI), which has been flexible but lacked strong guarantees and sample efficiency, by combining contraction-based closed-loop rollouts with discrete-time barrier function runtime verification.

The derived finite-sample stochastic stability bound clearly separates the effect of increasing samples from physical disturbances and modeling errors. Furthermore, simulation results across three distinct dynamical systems—a rover, a quadrotor, and a spacecraft—consistently demonstrated superior tracking performance and complete safety.

By injecting rigorous stability and safety into sampling control without compromising its flexibility to handle non-smooth cost functions, this framework establishes a powerful foundation for model predictive control in uncertain robotics environments.

takeaways: Running contraction feedback inside rollouts instead of open-loop rollouts uniformly prevents sample dispersion regardless of horizon length, dramatically boosting sample efficiency.

Because importance-weighted control inputs can cross non-convex safety boundaries, an execution layer that checks and corrects the input with a quantile-tightened DCBF right before execution is extremely effective.
Control input error from a finite sample size $N_s$ decreases at $O(N_s^{-1/2})$ and can be explicitly bounded as a floor on closed-loop tracking error.
An architecture combining Riccati-based contraction theory with MPPI's ability to evaluate non-smooth costs (such as $\ell_0$ norms and discontinuous penalties) holds immense practical value.
limitations: Requires offline computation to solve Riccati equations along reference trajectories and verify Jacobian contraction across the domain.
The theoretical closed-loop tracking error bound derived in Theorem 1 is quite conservative (roughly 500 to 650 times larger than simulated values), making it loose for practical gain tuning.

The execution layer assumes the existence of a valid backup policy (Assumption 5), leaving recoverability checks reliant on online heuristics if severe disturbances or sudden environmental changes render the backup infeasible.
